Hacknet is a cyberpunk-themed hacking simulation game that places players in the role of a hacker tasked with completing various digital missions. Dive into the world of computer systems, uncover secrets, and navigate a web of challenges in a realistic and immersive experience. The game blends puzzle-solving, strategy, and a deep narrative to keep players engaged.

[b]Key Features:[/b]

[b]Hacking Simulation:[/b] Hacknet offers a unique and authentic hacking experience, where players utilize a variety of commands and tools to infiltrate systems. The realistic simulation of a hacker's environment adds an extra layer of depth and immersion.

[b]Narrative-Driven Gameplay:[/b] The game features an engaging story where players uncover a conspiracy as they hack into various systems. The narrative unfolds through emails and logs, enhancing the sense of mystery and intrigue as the player progresses.

[b]Puzzle-Solving Mechanics:[/b] Each mission in Hacknet presents complex puzzles that require players to think critically and use their skills. The puzzles become progressively more challenging, adding a sense of accomplishment upon completion.

[b]Cyberpunk Atmosphere:[/b] Hacknet captures the essence of a cyberpunk world, with its gritty visuals and electronic soundscape. The game's aesthetic is minimalistic but effective, contributing to the overall tension and immersion.

[b]Realistic Hacking Tools:[/b] Players are equipped with a variety of hacking tools and software that mimic real-world techniques. The need to learn and adapt to new tools and strategies is a key aspect of the gameplay.

[b]Time-Sensitive Missions:[/b] Players must act quickly to complete missions before their actions are detected. This adds an element of urgency and excitement to the gameplay, pushing players to work efficiently under pressure.

[b]Conclusion:[/b] Hacknet stands out as an immersive and engaging hacking simulation game that captures the essence of a cyberpunk world. Its narrative, puzzle-solving mechanics, and realistic hacking tools provide a captivating experience for players who enjoy strategy, problem-solving, and an atmospheric gaming environment. The game's unique approach to hacking and its strong narrative make it a memorable experience in the cyberpunk genre.

review_text_raw:
I believe this review to be my first, and let me say this: Hacknet is the most fun I've had with a piece of interactive media in a very long time. It oozes with immersion and masterclass functionality. After Portal 2, most people were left wandering aimlessly along the dunes of the puzzle genre. From time to time, there was an innovative incorporation of puzzle-elements, but never something so powerful. 

GNU/Linux is a UNIX-based mobile, server, office and home desktop operating system. It is built on the powerful and lightning-fast Linux kernel developed by Linus Torvalds in 1996. It's destiny was to maximize productivity and hasten the process of technological evolution. Being lightweight and monolithic, you can take Linux with you wherever you go. When you thought of the internet, you always heard about Linux ever so briefly. 

But recently, things have begun to change. As the corporation gains more control over what we've known to be the internet, people are becoming more concerned. The people want more control over what they rightfully own. Linux offers a full computer suite capable of doing everything a Windows system can do in its own way. This makes Linux a functional choice for people looking for a way out. 

To see such a beautiful piece of technology incorporated into a hacking simulator is beautiful. It's all done so faithfully too. The more I play, the more excited I get. It's fluid, only ever needing so much RAM to operate smoothly. It's also quite responsive, despite some animations taking a lot longer than they should honestly. Another minor flaw is the fact that there's no currency system. There's really only ranking as a reward. It would be cool to make some money and purchase upgrades or better tools.

My final gripe is that some of the missions get a little repetitive. But the story balances things out by keeping it all fresh. There will be funny conversations you can find throughout each system. There's also interesting hide-and-seek style treasure hunts. Listening to cyberpunk playlists really help bring the vibe forward. The interface is extremely realistic.

There was no need to go any further, everything is heavily inspired by an actual personal home desktop Linux installation. The desktop environment in this game gives me an i3-gaps vibe. I could be wrong. I'm just playing this on Linux and being amazed and how honest it feels. 

I wish you could change the wallpaper, the colors, and maybe even the font of your interface. It would make the game feel more personal and exciting. Imagine hacking on a cute hello kitty desktop! <3

review_text_raw:
This is gonna be a lengthy review. I'll add a TL;DR at the bottom.

When I first went to view the page for this game, there were many questions that began flooding my mind. And now that I've played the game almost to its entirety, I think that I can answer most of these questions that interested consumers passing by may have. This game was a real treat, and I think that it deserves more attention than it's received.


[h1] Is Hacknet realistic? [/h1]

If you mean "realistic" as in "Is this game close to hacking in real life?" then the answer is no. This game is not realistic because it is fun and doesn't make you paranoid. You are in possession of a bunch of hacking tools that put up the kinds of graphics you'd expect to be running on computers in a 90's hacker film, and the way these tools work is by executing them and waiting for the flashy hacking graphics to stop flashing so that you can run another flashy hacker tool until you gain administrative system access. Granted, it's more complex than that, which is why this game is really enjoyable, but you're not going to be writing complex algorithms to overload proxy servers and bypass tracing measures. That's what the 90's tools are for.

That being said, this may be as close as gaming will ever come to realistic hacking. Because anything that tries to be precicely like real hacking that doesn't give you fancy hacker programs probably isn't going to be a very fun game. And this, again, is a fun game. The entire game takes place on a computer's operating system, and every hack you perform is done through this system. In addition, the commands you use are based on real UNIX commands, even if the commands are typically used to activate the previously-mentioned hacking programs. It's certainly more realistic than games where you push a button and your character goes [i]"I'm in" [/i] like Watch_Dogs and Quadrilateral Cowboy (That isn't to say that they're bad games, just that they're not trying to be realistic hacking simulations which, again, isn't necessarily a bad thing).


[h1] Is this game immersive? Will I feel like a hacker even if I'm not performing real hacks? [/h1]

Oh, yes. If you want to feel like the genius hacker that always appears in Hollywood films but rarely gets any time for actual character development, then this game is for you. The presentation of this game is great, and it really helps to sell that feeling of accomplishment that you get when you pull off a successful job. After about 30 minutes in, I had to re-check the steam store to make sure that I wasn't accessing a multiplayer hacking simulator. But nope, I was even able to play this game in airplane mode. As the store page mentions, there are very few things that break the immersion by being obvious parts of a video game. To complete a job, you email the client explaining that you've finished. To acquire a new tool, you have to copy said tool to your home computer from its rightful owner. 

And this immersive presentation goes a long way in the overall experience. I know that not everybody responds the same way, but I found certain parts to incite genuine emotion in a way that few other games have managed to pull off. Like when you're given the option to accept a job in which [spoiler]you have to euthanize a dying man by hacking his pacemaker [/spoiler], or when [spoiler]you run "OpenCDtray" on your own system and your real computer's disc tray opens and may potentially scare the hell out of you[/spoiler]. So even if you're using overpowered tools to open systems that nobody bothers to check, you'll probably still feel really good doing so.


[h1] Do I need to know coding or hacking in order to understand this game? [/h1]

No, you don't. The tutorial explains everything pretty well, and it makes sure that you understand how the systems work before even thinking about letting you out into the hacking world. No coding is required (I'm not even sure if coding algorithms is possible with the interface), and most of the game's difficulty comes with memorizing the commands and executing them at the appropriate times. That being said, if you don't know a whole lot about computers, the most difficult task will probably be [spoiler] getting your interface back after being locked to terminal mode by another hacker [/spoiler]. But if you experiment enough, then you'll ususally find the solutions to most of the challenges, and there are plenty of walkthroughs and tips out there if you end up getting desperate. But I was able to finish the game with little prior programming experience. If you know how to navigate a computer's interface or have downloaded and fixed mods on to other games, then you'll probably be fine with this game. Just, you know, don't delete important files or screw up on a trace aversion. I don't know if this game prevents you from screwing yourself over, and everybody's too scared to find out.


[h1] Is the game worth ten bucks? [/h1]

Yeah, I'd say so. You'll probably get around 10 hours out of it if you're doing the main story without any outside assitance, 14-15 hours if you're also doing the labrynths DLC. I'd say that it's not everybody's cup of tea; surely, your relative who spends all day exclusively playing [i] Fortnite [/i] would probably get turned off by this, but odds are you're at least mildly interested in this game if you're reading this review right now, considering that this game gets talked about as much as what brand of toilet paper you prefer when you're finished up on the toilet. So yeah, I'd recommend this game to anybody reading this review.


[h1] Oh, boy. It's one of those games that tries to sell its soundtrack as DLC. Is it good enough to warrant a purchase? [/h1]

I was honestly surprised by this game's soundtrack. Again, I understand that everybody has different tastes in music, but I found this particular OST track good to write and do homework to. It felt really good to listen to in-game while hacking servers and computers. The music is used as sort of an indicator on what part of the game you're currently at, and when the song changes, you know you're probably making progress. I found that [spoiler] Roller Mobster by Carpenter Brut [/spoiler] fit this game better than it did for HM2. That being said, I haven't purchased the soundtrack since most of it is available on YouTube anyways. And yes, it's ten dollars. Fifteen dollars for the main game and DLC soundtrack. So while I'll admit that the soundtrack is pretty good, I'd only spend the extra fifteen bucks if you like having the songs directly at your fingertips at all times.


[h1] TL;DR [/h1]

This is a great game that may be as close to realistic hacking as gaming will come while still remaining enjoyable. The presentation and aeshetic really add a lot to it, and you don't need to be experienced with programming or hacking in order to complete it. It's worth the money and gives around 10 hours of playtime assuming you don't mess up massively and have to start a new game. I'm gonna give this a thumbs up, and I wish it came out later so that I could put it in my favorite 2018 games list.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very unique genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. [/h1]

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc.

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it.

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into.

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into.

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look around some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you. The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look around some and find every secret I suspect. NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

review_text_raw:
Cool Concept, But It Couldn’t Keep Me Hooked

Hacknet starts strong. The idea of diving into a terminal-based hacking sim with a mysterious narrative hook is instantly appealing, especially if you’re into cyberpunk aesthetics or want to feel like a digital detective. At first, typing out real commands and navigating the virtual systems feels immersive and fresh. But that feeling didn’t last long for me.

The main problem is how quickly the novelty wears off. After a couple of missions, the gameplay loop becomes repetitive — scan, probe, crack, read a few emails, rinse and repeat. There’s little variety or meaningful evolution in the mechanics. You’re not solving clever puzzles so much as going through the motions of the same routine over and over.

The story, while intriguing in concept, never really grabbed me. It’s told in fragments through logs and emails, but it lacks emotional weight or urgency. I never felt particularly invested in the characters or their motivations — and a lot of the writing just felt flat.

On top of that, there are some pacing issues. Some tasks feel tedious and drawn out, while others jump ahead abruptly. And if you’re not already familiar with basic command-line structure, the early learning curve can feel more frustrating than fun.

I really wanted to like Hacknet. It nails the aesthetic and tone, and I respect the ambition. But the shallow gameplay and underwhelming story made it feel more like a tech demo than a fully satisfying experience.

review_text_raw:
I'd only recommend this game if: you get it for free or really cheap, you want a short game to play but don't care what, or you just really want to see lots of scrolling lines and feel like a faux hacker

Otherwise, I don't think it's worth your time for the following reasons:

1. too simple and repetitive
Once you figure out the command lines after a few minutes that's the entire game play. In fact, you'll have to type the same things over so many times you'll mostly use the GUI menu instead. Then, you just wait around all the time waiting for the same 4-5 port hacks to finish that's nothing more than progress bars and flashing numbers like you see in movies. You do this again and again over the next few hours doing simple contracts you pick up from the hacker group postings board (which don't require any thinking since they tell you exactly where to go and what to do which is most of the time just deleting some files off the target server). 

2. lack of story and immersion
As mentioned above, 90% of the time you are doing these simple job postings. The other 10% is the actual story but other than a quick introduction to the missing dead hacker in the beginning, all of its related missions are shoehorned at the end in like the last three missions. Also, another problem I had was the immersion. If you read the files in the folders they want you to target, they're related to the back story of the mission you're doing but if you poke around in the home folder they're just a bunch of random files. For example, it doesn't make sense to read irc chat logs of teenagers making dumb pun jokes and a grocery list in an enterprise server.

3. some poor ui choices
Every IP address you visit is pinned on a board as a node that you can revisit at anytime. However, the nodes become very cluttered towards the end of the game, and critical story nodes at the end are overlapped with a bunch of nodes you visited at the start of the game. I got stuck for a bit for one mission because when I scanned for connected networks I could not see the one out of the five that newly showed up which I needed to go to. It really didn't help that the countdown timer (active trace, which I'll talk about below) was right on top of that region, blocking my view. Lastly, there's something about the background and font color choice and or the font size that is eye straining and made me feel nauseous at times. Made me want to skim through the text a lot of the times.

4. feature bypass/abuse
There's a gameplay feature called active trace which is basically a countdown timer before the server tracks you down because it knows it's being hacked. Fun idea in theory but it's only ever a threat once in the game. Every other time you can circumvent it by hacking the server then disconnecting, then when you reconnect you can login as admin because it saved the password somehow from just hacking the ports. At this point you can leisurely scroll through the server and not worry about getting caught. If you do run out the timer and get caught you go into fail safe mode where you have a limited time to change your ip address but I just rebooted the virtual OS and that "solves" the problem.

review_text_raw:
[h1]What to expect if you're new to this game genre[/h1]
Hacknet is a new title in the otherwise stagnant, indie genre of hacking simulation games.
And a fresh breeze it is.

No doubt there is hardly any competition for this kind of quality.
Graphics are amazing, the hacking system introduced is quite good and consistent, it has gigantic potential for expansion that desperately needs to be used, and hopefully will. In it's current shape there might be little room for multiplayer gameplay, because of the game mechanics, but hopefully as the game gets finalized it will be implemented.

The puzzles you have to face are fun to solve and most of the time at medium or easy difficulty level.
Even though the game description provided on Steam might be a little misleading, as to non-holywood hacking style, or minimal hand-holding, the gameplay can be extremely exciting and satisfying.
The thrill of hacking, taking unauthorised control over websites, other web services, or user machines and mobile devices, identity theft or destruction, and constantly racing the trace clock are all very satisfying and will give you an addictive adrenaline rush.

Music is a very proper and enjoyable background for your virtual crimes, not quite something to remember.

The game has too high hardware requirements in my opinion. All in all it is a console based hacking game, and it is barely playable on i5, 4GB, Intel graphics HD4000 Lenovo laptop (12 fps max with too much typing lag!!!)

[h1]Finally the 'Uplink vs Hacknet'[/h1]
Many people look up to Hacknet in comparison to Uplink.
Based on my experiences with both titles If you did truly enjoy Uplink, You will be dazzled by Hacknet's modern design. Graphics are eyecandy.
The gameplay itself however, as compared to Uplink I have found to be short (if that can be said - I was unable to finish the game due to numerous bugs [despite 50+hrs in-game]), shallow and at many times unchallenging.
If you can bear with, well kinda outdated graphics and a little clumsy UI, I'd say Uplink offers far greater immersion, much more complex world to explore, more freedom, less hand holding.
Hardware upgrades covering several computer components to your machine, or even different, more upgradable machines (you can create them yourself or download one of many community created ones!!!!), software upgrades that all can be purchased are something you won't find in Hacknet, since finances have been taken out of the picture in the first place. Money earning, stock market participation and manipulation, and banking are all absent in Hacknet. So are LAN networks that pose a sublevel of gameplay in Uplink. Hacknet at this stage of developement also gives you the feeling of being the only web user out there, since only on rare story related events will you ever find logs left by anyone else on any servers (even the public services). Tracing other hackers or users is nearly non existent since the idea of connection bouncing has also been skipped so far. In my opinion, with similar development times of several years for both games, Uplink is a masterpiece bot technically and story-wise, compared to Hacknet.

[h1]Final words[/h1]
Whatever Hacknet is or will be, I'd say Uplink is worth playing, as the only other hacking game out there with some serious gameplay to this date.
If compatibility issues or the kinda-outdated-look are an obstacle for you playing Uplink, Hacknet will still be a very enjoyable and exciting experience, however I would strongly advise to wait with the purchase until numerous major bugs are addressed and more potential gets released from Hacknet, or you might be facing quite a frustrating struggle with what I can only call a beta version (at best) right now. I have also learned there is a free remake of Uplink to be found out there, I will let you find it yourself tho, since I'd stick with the original version by Introversion Software and support it's makers.
Keep track of Hacknet news and discussion on Steam for a stable version somewhen in the (hopefully) near future.

So after playing for a short while and considering my interest in cyber security, this game does really pull you into a different perspective altogether, especially if you're unaware of the concept behind malicious activities. This game puts you straight into the seat of a hacker, where cracking, executing and advanced computer knowledge is your weapon as you progress through the story in stages. At the start of the story, you begin in a tutorial stage which walks you through basic commands and how to hack a port and delete tracking information. As well as disconnecting from systems. The tutorial is well constructed and written, which helps the player understand what to do and how to do something to advance. The story also has no voice acting, but relies on text as if some anonymous user is contacting you - an example would be the in-game email system and intermissions. When it comes to presentation, it definitely makes you feel a part of something outside your comfort zone, as the hacking environment really does look and feel as if you're breaching unsecure or secured networks.

Overall, Hacknet doesn't fail to impress me and it's worth checking out if you're into cyber security or computer coding.

Wow, Hacknet is one immersive command line game.
You get to pick up the left overs of a now dead hacker, following in his footsteps, slowly taking on harder challenges and making a name for yourself.
Hacknet offers a tight narrative (which is completely text based) and enthralling 'hacking'

Pros:
 - presentation. I know a lot of people will be turned off by a CL interface game. but heck (huehue), it's beautiful, intuitive and well designed. plus you can download more UIs from servers and people you hacked
 - gameplay. it's relatively easy, requiring (so far, I'm roughly 4 hours into the game) simple management skills, a keen eye and some reading and prioritizing. the hacking is served well, not letting you button mash, but rather focused on the finer points such as: reading emails for usernames and passwords, changing websites headers into vulgarities, finding the right tools and balance, covering your tracks.
     a lot of the gameplay is indeed done over a command line interface, which, exactly, means you type out what you wanna do. there's helps, and little tools making it a lot easier than real life hacking could ever be.
- Story. it's a pretty cool mix of paranoia, technology and a weird form of justice. no one talks, no fancy cutscenes. it's all in your head, buddy
 - immersion. yeah, the computers you hack are rather empty, but what is on there is hilarious and often gives small hints to connections between the hackers you 'meet' (I think, at least
 - music. absolutely perfect. 

Cons:
 - uhm, let me think ... hmmm ... no, it is exactly what it says it is. and then some

Verdict:

You like hacking/hacking movies or just recently discovered Mr Robot or the deep web?
Well, come on in. this is a perfect supplement to your diet.
Hacknet is pretty (for CL standards :D as I work in IT I actually find it gorgeous), fun and fast paced. It will test your patience, but mostly your ability to read and type properly.
But nothing is keeping it from delivering the best hacker game since Uplink, if not even a tick better.
And it is totally worth the price tag

review_text_raw:
[h1] Hacknet [/h1]
[b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b]

[h1] Run-through [/h1]

Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web.

With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

• Amazing story
• Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up
• Challenging and entertaining puzzles
• The music feels always on point with the situation
• Mod support
• Tons of fun little Easter Eggs

[h1] Cons: [/h1]

• The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre
• As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences

[h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1]

[u][b] General information [/b][/u]
Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job.

Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere.

There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth.

Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program.

The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games.

Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there.

[u][b] Content [/b][/u]
Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay.

[h1] Technical Analysis [/h1]

[u][b] Graphics [/b][/u]
A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else.
Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text.

[u][b] Music [/b][/u]
For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions.

[u][b] HUD [/b][/u]
The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable.
To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other.

[u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u]
None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done.

[h1] Wrapping up [/h1]

Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for.

review_text_clean: [h1] Hacknet [/h1] [b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b] [h1] Run-through [/h1] Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web. With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines. [h1] Pros: [/h1] • Amazing story • Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up • Challenging and entertaining puzzles • The music feels always on point with the situation • Mod support • Tons of fun little Easter Eggs [h1] Cons: [/h1] • The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre • As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences [h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1] [u][b] General information [/b][/u] Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job. Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere. There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth. Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program. The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games. Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there. [u][b] Content [/b][/u] Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay. [h1] Technical Analysis [/h1] [u][b] Graphics [/b][/u] A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else. Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text. [u][b] Music [/b][/u] For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions. [u][b] HUD [/b][/u] The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable. To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other. [u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u] None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done. [h1] Wrapping up [/h1] Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for. review_text_raw:
Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

[h1]WARNING this review will have spoilers, however, I've already marked what I consider to be spoilers[/h1]

This review is [b]NOT[/b] for people who plan on going through this game and only doing what the scripts you to. This is for those who want to delete everything they can get into after downloading files that they'd like to save as trophies or blackmail.

This is a great game, I have yet to beat it but I've loved most of the time I've put into this game, which is why I'm sad to say that I can't recommend this game. My main issue with it is the fact that its dead, unless I'm mistaken which is very possible. This game is filled with hand placed text and files as well as scripted events. At one point in the game, towards the beginning, [spoiler]you have to hack into a clicker game (that you can actually play which is super cool!) in order to delete an elite player's save so that he can show off his clicker power once more! I deleted the entire game alongside EVERYONE's saves. If you choose to do this you don't need to fret, you can still play the game, which is the main issue... WHY CAN I PLAY A DELETED GAME?[/spoiler] This trend follows with pretty much any computer or server you hack into, no one reacts, nothing gets repaired over time and things still work... WHY? Why does no one care if I've deleted ALL their system files, why do things still work even after I've deleted the file that basically says "DO NOT DELETE OR WILL STOP WORKING!!!" And why can't I blackmail people? I probably won't be able to get myself to beat this game because it just feels dead to me, sure its a lot of fun, but the immersion is killed the second I try to jump ship and do my own thing.

A second issue some people may have with this game is that it expects you to know, or figure out, everything outside of the few basic things it teachs you from the start, sometimes while being put under the clock. I have no real gripes with this, the game doesn't hold your hand (which I like), the only reason I mentioned it was for those players who don't like being forced to figure out solutions they've never been taught.

tl;dr: This game is dead, do anything outside of the script and its like nothing happened and no one cares. Make sure you can think on your feet and make sure you don't mind finding solutions to problems you've never even seen before.

review_text_raw:
The game design works at first, and there are timed missions when you really get into the action – musics do their job. You have kind of a sense of accomplishment as you get your hands on more "hacking" tools and get to face bigger challenges. There is quite a lot of humorous content on the side – not in the main story! – and that's appreciated because it's not far from being a text game.

But that's about all the nice things I can think about this game. Pretty soon, you reach its limits and the sense of accomplishment fades away. If you have no feeling for IT stuff, you may get lost pretty fast. But if you're too much into it, the game mechanisms are very disappointing. The main idea was good, but the execution rather bad. If you're still curious, I'd suggest to buy it on sale.

The difficulty relies on: 1. The cryptic aspect of computers – you'd better know the basics about file system and console ;  2. Timed challenges ; 3. Finding little bits of information (user name, password, IP...) here and there among text in files and mail ; 4. Systematically scan the targets in all ways possible. That's not something that keeps one entertained for long.

The console, which you use a lot, is rather rudimentary. At the very least it should have felt like a real one and at least to go smoothly when you type. The cursor is glitchy, not always showing where it actually is. Key pushes may be repeated when hold a few microseconds too long. The number of commands is very limited. They are sometimes buggy when not used as intended. Managing the in-game files is pretty tedious, there are no commands for creating/deleting directories. There is no way to make scripts or shortcuts. At best you can rename the executables. By the way, having "exe" files on a Linux simulation is an heresy.

The graphic interface lacks functionalities too. It would be great if you could move and resize the panels, especially the one for the "netmap" which gets pretty packed and hard to read after a while. You may find an in-game executable which helps a little bit with that. Also content will overflow from panels when too big. Why no copy/paste available?!? It would have been so useful. I grew tired of retype every user name, password and IP. Plus there are some links that are meant to be open in a real browser (as eater eggs only).

The game mechanisms are very limited. Some special missions or events break the monotony, but the player are not prepared for them either. [spoiler]For instance you are not likely to be able to defend your computer against other hackers.[/spoiler] The hacking tools are also limited in number, in versions and they almost all work in the same way. Missions are quite alike, and you're doing the same dull things over, and over, and over...

They tried to make up for it with the game story, but it turns out to be a bit déjà vu, corny, and even a bit predictable.

Two alternatives would have been preferable for making such a game:
— Either make it more approachable, even less realistic but with a more pleasant game design. Then it would need hacking to be more like puzzles.
— Or make a game for nerds, where the in-game computers can be configured, where files matter, with better console commands and executables, even maybe some scripts to edit.

review_text_raw:
The game's unique mechanics and addictive storyline make it an absolute pleasure to play.

One of the things I love most about Hacknet is how immersive it is. The game does an incredible job of making you feel like a real hacker with its realistic interface and authentic hacking commands. It's a game that not only entertains but also educates on the intricacies of hacking.

The gameplay itself is challenging but rewarding. Each mission requires careful planning and execution, forcing you to think outside the box to achieve your goals. review_text_raw:
HACKNET - 7/10

Quick Review: A "hacking simulator" with gameplay akin to getting your first DOS system up and running, Hacknets weak story doesn't hold back the interesting and ever expanding gameplay.

Story
------
You, an amateur hacker, are contacted by someone named "Bit", who gives you an extra tool to add to your hacking repertoire and from there the expansive world is open to you. Using your new found tools, you become a part of something greater, helping (obviously shady) people with your hacking skills while trying to figure out just what the hell the Hacknet really is, and it might be more dangerous than you thought...

Overall, unfortunately the story is the weakest point. Everything is told through text in the game and the story really only starts to open up and become explained by the end but by that time you're more than likely burnt out from your constant reading. Most of the game has you completing irrelevant odd jobs for obvious scum with little relevance to the story, which is why the story is the weakest part.

Gameplay
-----------
Gameplay of Hacknet involves 2 things: typing and hacking. Your UI is a command window with a display of the target computer in the center, all the devices you have access to at the bottom and the command console on the right. Basic gameplay goes like this: Select a PC you want to hack, you "probe" it (by typing "probe") which will display a list of security measures. You then type whatever relevant command you need for the security measure (theres about 6 different types and you'll get the tools required as you progress through the game), wait a bit for it to be hacked, than do whatever it is the quest needs you to do; either copy a file to your system, delete a file, edit a file, find an ip address and send it to the client etc. The entire game revolves around typing commands and clicking files.

I do think the gameplay is fun however, it has to be for me to give it a 7/10. By the time you get the hang of your newly introduced command, you'll learn yet another and another until you get near the end. There is alot you can do and quite alot of secrets to find as you make your way through the story. The gameplay at it's core is simple but it takes a while to memorise all the power you have.

Design
-------
The UI for the game is great, and the gameplay experience really makes you feel like H4CK3RM@NZ.  You get access to different coloured themes as you progress, and alot of the files you can find on the computers are quite hilarious. The soundtrack is a banger too, and the end of the game features some of the best final music i've ever heard.

Problems
----------
It's a simple game, so it has simple problems. Alot of the text files you find on computers are just copy pasted across many devices, filling them up so you spend more time browsing through them than needed. There was a bit too much waiting involved when it came to hacking and required almost 0 thought, you simply type the command for whatever hacking tool you need and the number that corresponds with it, then you wait. The biggest problem I have is that as you get further and further in the game, the amount of devices you can access starts to clutter your device map. Because devices are represented as circles with no names, I spent ages hovering over 30+ circles trying to find what computer I was looking for, and they end up overlapping sometimes too. This sometimes made me have to re-hack into a previous computer to find the IP for the computer I wanted to hack into even if I already had it available, simply because it was impossible to find on my device map.

Achievements
---------------
The achievements are....relatively easy and can be gotten in 1 playthrough but you need to know what to do without the game telling you. You need to discover quite a few secrets and go out of your way to get alot of the achievements but there isn't an enormous amount of content in the game so as long as you try and explore everything you'll probably get them.

Summary
----------
A super unique experience and nothing like i've ever played. The banging soundtrack and addictive gameplay makes me easily recommend this, but only if you can overlook it's numerous, but not awful problems.

Also I can't stress enough the end of the game. It's seriously, SERIOUSLY amazing and worth playing just to experience it. Everything about it is great and the song that plays alongside it couldn't have been more perfect...for anything.

review_text_raw:
Yes, yes, yes, more of this please.

Where are all the DLCs? We need more! There's only one DLC, really?!

Great game with a good story and in-game terminal activities, however it could use a refresh. It's kind of stuck in the 90's, but I loved it all the same. I didn't like all the MS Win homage within a Linux or Unix terminal game. It's a simple version of the rich Linux OS (or Unix) and it's tools as well as the network concept. Which is fine, however the breaking into systems kind of gets old after the third or forth try. You learn that you have to acquire the tool for the job (port) and that's it. You acquire tools as you go, and you "steal" tools as you progress, but it's really simple. It's great all the same, just needs a few adjustments and improvements.

I though you could sell all that data or exchange it for tools, so I kept some of it from the big jobs, I ended up with a tone of stuff in / and /home, never being able to do anything with it.

What the game misunderstands, but makes easy on the player is:
- Unix and Linux binary files don't end in exe and don't use PE format, they use ELF.
- braking firewalls and proxy (well VPN servers) is not that easy and doesn't require any memory on the client/hacker side
- tracing a hacker is done differently, one could kick a user from his machine but not trace him in that way or that fast
- buffer overflow is simplistic and unimaginative 
- the memory concept could've been done differently with memory updates, etc. I expected more, it's just there to make your work slower so the tracer could kick in.
- Unix commands are not uppercase, and are case sensitive (I know, I know, I'm pushing it)
- firewalls and proxys are just there to make you slower, no concept of network or network security

Other Cons:
- no vi (yeah, I kept tying it all the same, and wondered why it didn't work), you have to use cat, replace
- you cannot create folders, no mkdir, which is weird
- no vi so, text editing, you have to kind of use replace, which works for the mostpart
- no touch, so you cannot make new files
- no shell scripts (shell is just a different concept all together)
- /home/ doesn't have a user, AT ALL
- root is admin
- no concept of mount or a filesystem
- no killall command
- there are no routers (because the game acts like we are in the 90's, but there are software firewalls and proxys)
- no VPN concept within the proxy
- no ssh shelling to the other machines and attacking from that machine (override doesn't count, you still have your own IP)
- ssh is just there because
- there are no worms, viruses or rootkits
- forkbomb is just a hard reboot
- the trigger/trap is a waste, you just need it once and never again, you don't even have to have the shells open in the other parts of the game and in the DLC
- the music, although OK for the mostpart, it's a little to digital for me and I kind of require more tones, metal or rock would 
suffice
- there are a few good tracks which have melody inside
- the game hinders CPU extensively (I'm playing it on Linux and this shouldn't happen), it could use with some optimization. I didn't notice this until I minimized the game, or went to shell to do something and saw the CPU cores all at 100% all the while the game was suspended, which is strange. I don't know how it was written, but these things only happen with Javascript.
- the IRC logs are old and outdated, from bash.org
- why do we even have IRC without being able to log and hack it?
- hexclock just randomly changes color as the time ticks, instead of being able you use -s or -n, which don't do anything, to change the hex color yourself.
- not all the save files sync via cloud for me, so I could not enjoy it on different machines, and had to copy the save files manually
- you cannot change the layout of the theme, switch the windows around and change color, leaving you with unwanted colors and layout for most of the time
- DLC themes are better than the original game
- Honeypot theme (you know which server I'm talking about) is just the GOLD theme - which you can acquire before attacking that server
- you don't have to actually delete the logs, it's just so you can complete the job
- no world interaction whatsoever, feels like the machines you break in have no owner and have been sitting there for ages (only one or two cases are dangerous, if we include the DLC, you will actually have to remain unnoticed, rest of the time you can do whatever you like) 
- even though the story starts good, the plot kind of goes off into another corner
- the hacknet program does nothing, and is just there for the plots sake, or in reference to the actual game binary
- there is no concept of money, you just hack for the sake of it
- DLC starting requires research, you have to start it via in-game plot points (it's triggered after you end the game, but it's stated no where how to turn it on)

Pros
- everything else is pro, which is alot
- you can scan for other machines within the network
- the terminal only theme and the network nods make it a great visual pleasure (for us Linux users at least)
- there are secrets within the game
- there are some pieces of the game that will make you feel like you're in a movie
- there are some well though out scenarios - including the DLC
- iOS, or eOS is present, so mobile hacking is possible although very simple and dull
- mobile hacking, pacemaker hacking, other medical devices (although they use the same tool)
- server secrets
- secret servers :D
- great ending (and DLC continuation)
- Neo? - or did I make a mistake (you know what I mean)
- there are some text files or manual documentation for the tools
- you can hack your ISP provider as well
- you can hack almost anything, with a few machines left unbreakable, I won't spoil it
- DLC is really good, so get that too

Advice:
Rename all your commands to the Unix style (all Linux people know what I'm saying) and be lightning fast and untraceable. That's what I did along with placing everything in / and not /home/ which doesn't have a user and is just weird.

Now make yourself some coffee and hack.

Enjoy.

review_text_raw:
This game is good. Just not great.

I actually didn't finish this game, but I read a story synopsis and it was, well, not too creative. Decent, but not amazing. The reason I didn't finish is because the story effectively takes a break for about 8-10 hours after the first hour, having you invest into smaller stories that you come across in small missions. The other reason I didn't finish was that the gameplay felt like actual hacking and work, and it was the kind of grindy, difficult work that one might receive in a classroom. Some features of the UI were extremely difficult to operate, and while that was somewhat realistic, I came to play a game, not because I liked doing difficult computer work, which is part of the reason why some hackers become hackers. Speaking of that, this game makes hacking extremely easy and simplified. I guess that if a hacking OS was developed in real life, it may actually be this easy, but in reality now hacking is way more difficult, complicated and sometimes more fun than this.

The world building and details were fantastic. I can't tell you how many times I laughed scrolling through logs on PCs I'd hacked into. They were well written and funny. But the massive break from the story made me feel like I was actually doing hacker work (although way too easy) and not playing a game. I came to experience a story, play a game, be something and someone else for a while, not to actually do hacker work. This game did not advertise as a hacker sim, but as a game where you play as a hacker with a story. That is my main problem with this game.

And don't get me wrong--I am all about games that require you do think and reflect and do not have big visuals or explosions or gunfights--this game's gameplay was boring. I've already said how the hacking was too easy and the UI was way too hard, but simply, hacking got boring rather quickly. That's basically it. In terms of additional information, there were no bugs and it was programmed very solidly. 

Overall, get this game when it is very cheap and play it for a few hours. You can have more fun with it than just two hours, so you don't have to return it, just buy it very cheap or free, that's how I got this game, it was free for a limited time and I downloaded it. 79/100 -- good, just not a B.

review_text_raw:
[b]A HACKER GROUP SEARCHING THE TRUTH[/b]
[i]Hacknet[/i] was available for free in Humble Bundle for a short period, long time ago. It's one of those game that normally I wouldn't buy. The game is centered on group of hackers that receives some contracts from people that wants to obtain something: it could be retrieving a file or cancel something from another user computer. For the entire game, you will see the Hacknet OS, a system that allows to execute some tools and let you inside other networks and devices.

[h1]VERY REPETITIVE GAMEPLAY[/h1]
At the beginning [i]Hacknet[/i] seems promising. The game make you feel like you are a real hacker, trying to break in other people computers, but after a while everything repeat itself. You always do the same things: hack devices ports, with specific executables that you just need to download from the hacker group server, once you are in, you need to check the files, and once you completed the task, simply reply to the client request mail, with details needed. Some of these contract are challenging and it will take a lot of time, trying to understand which is the solution of the enigma. Usually there is not only one way to go, but you can complete the mission in different ways. The real problem is that missions are all the same and nothing really change for the whole game.

[h1]CANCEL THE LOGS[/h1]
One of the things that the game never stop to stress you out is deleting the logs in a computer after you finished to snoop around. At the beginning I did it, because I was scared that I could be traced, losing the mission. After a while, because you have so many steps to do in order to complete the contract, I forgot to clean them several times, and nothing happened. They cannot trace me so I simply stopped to worry about it: I canceled only when I remembered.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]
[i]Hacknet[/i] could have potential. It looks different and interesting, but, as I've mentioned before, you need to do always the same bunch of actions, and this made me lose the interest in the game. I have still to complete the main story, but I think I played enough to express an opinion on this title. I really wanted to buy also DLCs, but after this experience, I think I stop here my experience with this game.

review_text_raw:
[h1][i][b][u]Hacknet - 8/10[/u][/b][/i][/h1]

[u]Story[/u]
Hacknet is a puzzle game that focuses mainly on, well, hacking! At the very start of the game, you get a message from a person called "Bit", requesting a bit of hacking. [spoiler]He then, in a way, requests you to investigate his death.[/spoiler] There are also a bunch of "side" missions if you can call them that, to get good with a few other groups. I'm not saying anything else, go play it and experience it for yourself. The story is amazing and has a weird type of ending. Satisfying, though.
[spoiler]By the way, if you already know computer commands or you know how to hack, then you can skip the tutorial by writing "ps" once you get hold of the console and then "kill [i][Number shown beside "Tutorial"]"[/i][/spoiler]
[spoiler]You don't have to clear logs unless it tells you to do so in the mission briefing.[/spoiler]

[u]Storyline Length[/u]
This all depends on how good you are at puzzles, what knowledge you have of computer commands, and how fast you type. If you're great at all three of things, like me, then it should take you about an hour or two. There are quite a few tricky parts, so it might take you longer. If you're an achievement hunter, this will require at least two playthroughs to unlock all the achievements.

[u]AI[/u]
I'm not too sure if this counts as AI, but if you start to hack a really secure place, there's a chance you'll start to get traced. You have ninety seconds to finish up (and for some reason those 'ninety seconds' always go at a different speed) or else you have another minute or so to change your IP. Also, you can reply to emails and kill a guy or two but they don't really count as AI. Not in this game, anyway.

[u]Experience[/u]
This game will make you feel like a true hacker. Opening the ports of a secure server has never been easier with the programmes and knowledge you have! Firewalls? Not a problem! Proxy? Easy. 5 ports to open? Kindergarten stuff. This game, from start to finish, is a wild ride.  It'll make you laugh, make you make a hard decision even though you kinda have to do it one way, make you feel like everyone else is a peasant and you're the superior. You know, just like winning a round of CS:GO competitive against nine year olds. You can't have too many stuff open at once, which makes this game really challenging sometimes. Especially when you have to change your IP and you're extremely stressed. I'm not sure if you can move them around, I haven't tried, but the area where you decide where to connect to gets [i]extremely[/i] cluttered after a while. Would be great if you can delete some circles you're absolutely sure you won't connect to again.
Anyway, this thing actually runs on cmd which makes you feel even more of a hacker.
[spoiler]If you write "OpenCDTray" then it will open your actual computer's CD tray if you have one. Pretty damn cool![/spoiler]

[u]Graphics[/u]
Well, it's a computer desktop. Not much else to say. Deep into the game, you can get a theme changer, which changes your desktop in-game. That's about it, really.

[u]Sound[/u]
The soundtrack is not bad at all. It fits the game and can actually be quite relaxing! Although, you'll probably hear your keyboard half the time. Good stuff!

[u]Overall[/u]
I'd recommend this game to pretty much anyone. Especially those who love puzzle games, like me. This has a great story, challenging puzzles at times, and a great end. The achievements aren't too hard, but they're not too easy. Pick this up if you can, definitely worth €10.

[u]Specs[/u]
Well, it's a game that's literally cmd with a pretty desktop. I'm pretty sure the oldest computer on Earth could run this.

NVIDIA GeForce GTX 750 Ti
8GB RAM
Windows 7 (64 bit) Ultimate N
