review_text_raw:
While this game is being sold as a "hacking simulator", a debate will likely rage about what exactly it simulates. In either case, it comes suspiciously close to being a realistic simulation of hacking. So close, in fact, I'm left wondering why the dev didn't go the extra yards to make it inarguably so (maybe something he can shoot for in the future). Realism nit-picking aside, this game is full of very realistic nods to hacker and IRC culture, and in broad strokes, represents some of what goes on in actual exploits. While the experience of compromising systems is streamlined for the sake of keeping it an actual game (again, is it a puzzle game or a simulator?), in that "push a button, get bacon" sort of way you see in "hacker" movies, there was still much in the game that reminded me of taking the OSCP (for those who know my pain, you will find much in each mission to make you smile in that corpse-like rictus you had while laughing at emails and files during enumeration pratice in the Offsec lab).

After a while, I realized I was playing not so much because of the faux-hacking experience, but because there was a rather compelling story unfolding. Can't pick that apart without spoiling it, so I'll critique the gameplay instead (positives first):

[b]Pros:[/b]
This game is hilarious in a sick, twisted way. References to chan and IRC culture litter the storyline. While the majority of gameplay involves limited exploit combinations, there are moments where you don't know what the f**k is going on, and you have to think fast to avert a crisis. If you're into security culture, you'll find your intuition meshes well with the challenges, and you can improv what to do most of the time. It's like a Drunk History version of real hacking, so it's probably an ideal game to play while you're drunk.

People with zero knowledge of hacker culture or basic unix commands and quad notation will walk away familiar with all of the above.

The game is cheap, so whether you enjoy the simplistic, repetitive nature of the "hacking" it simulates, you won't regret the purchase, because it will entertain you regardless. The story itself is worth the price, and the way the story is told using the genre is clever.

If you liked TIS-100 (and I'm a recovering TIS-addict) you'll appreciate this for some of the same reasons, but the games aren't identical by a long shot. In fact, that would be the one constructive criticism I'd like both devs of these two games to hear: if TIS-100 had the narrative of Hacknet, and Hacknet had the coding fatures and complexity of TIS-100, you'd have a seriously ground breaking game on your hands, guys.

[i]Maybe the two of you should consider a collab or something...[/i]

[b]Cons:[/b]

Pushing buttons to get bacon gets fairly boring after a while, and the game loses some of its puzzle quality attributes as a result of the limited attack combinations, and the lack of customization or tweaking of exploits and tactics that is the real joy of hacking. If this was never going to be a hacking game, and more of a puzzle game, I wanted to see a complexity progression throughout, instead of a chaotic difficulty plataeu. 

[b]Also, why write so many missions for lelzsec, but make it so easy to permanently lose your chance to access them -- it was like a quarter of the game just gets skipped automagically because there isn't a clear choice presented to the player that an alternate path exists![/b]

Each mission certainly could have involved more manual hacks to achieve both realism and puzzle difficulty, but this would require adding more OS commands to the game, or a limited scripting engine of some sort. It couldn't have been that hard to add a mission where the solution was to exploit weak service permissions, tampering with programs launched by the OS at boot. Perhaps telling the print spooler to reset the system's admin password by re-writing it to launch a file with a "passwd" command in it, or to add a user account with "admin" privileges, something along these lines. A phishing mission, or getting a target to open an email and trigger a malicious trojan embedded in a PDF file would have been fun. These kinds of scenarios would require no "hacking tools", and might actually require the player to struggle. I'd rather struggle than push "exploit" over and over, my only real enemy being the trace timer.

To do this would require more system commands like "touch", privileges to edit, the ability to create files, maybe a basic word processor and the ability to write emails (instead of just reply... to some of them). All we had to work with were pre-existing files, a "replace" command that replaces lines and is too cumbersome, and no manner of scripting available. No complex chains of commands, no writing or editing code beyond some HTML (so I can change "chicken" to "c**ks", but that's not really hacking as much as being a d**k).

Once you get to that long slog of a valley mid-game, it stops feeling like hacking AND puzzle solving, and starts to feel more like grinding mobs in an MMO to get to the next bit of storyline. Each player will have more or less patience for that experience. Exploit tactics become routine too quickly, and the difficulty drops off.

[b]OVERALL[/b]:
Short game. In 20 hours you can play through twice and get all the achievements, and you compulsively will, despite the bugs that might force you to start a new game because something is glitched and can't recover [though the developer is working hard to patch all these, props to him]. There are enough Easter Eggs and humorous logs to make you anxious that you missed some the first time. More like an interactive novel for hackers than a puzzle game or simulator, but with elements of both; you will feel haunted putting together what your *actual* role in the missions might have been, and to what extent the Ayy Lmaos were involved. 

For $8-ish, I felt like I got more than I paid for and told my friends to play it for the lulz.

review_text_raw:
First things first, I loved the slick layout and visuals Hacknet plays quite nicely.  Music is pretty damn good too!

At first I really liked Hacknet as it feels like what Uplink should be in the modern gaming age.  You get cool looking interfaces, some psuedo-unix commands and maniplulations and a feeling of pressure as you hack your way past traces and logs.  However, thats where it falls apart a little.  You realise that logs are redundant and apart from an active trace when hacking some systems there are no repercussions to breaking log chains.  Except for one scripted event you dont need to worry about the men in black knocking on your door.  It was this attention to detail and consequnce that, in my opinion, gave Uplink its amazing gameplay.  I felt like the game needed that next level of complexity and difficulty to really come of age.

The major thumbs down however is game breaking bugs.  At time of writing this review there is at least one huge bug that is preventing the game being completed.  An attempt at fixing the bug was done but it did not solve the problem.  Cudos for the Developer at rushing to solve the issue but after one attempted patch there has been no communication on the status of the bug for about a month now.

Bottomline.  Its a fun little game but becomes one dimentional and easy once you realise there is no real way to lose apart from letting an active hack trace get you but even that is easily bypassed with one click or command.  The killer at this stage is bugs and more bugs.  I hope the game gets fixed and expanded, it could be a very nice game one day.


UPDATE:  The major bug has been fixed and I was able to finish the game.  Thanks to the Dev for fixing that up.
I have left my recommendation as negatvie which I am sad about as the game is pretty good.  The problem still is that its too easy once you realise there arent any repurcussions to not covering your tracks.  A little more depth would make this game a killer title!

review_text_raw:
"Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it. This creates a truly immersive experience and puts players right in the thick of trying to break through the firewalls."

Blatant lies. Hacknet is straight up Hollywood hacking. The terminal is a simplistic cross-breed between bash and cmd.exe. It puts you in the role of a script kiddy, who "hacks" systems by observing which ports are open on the target machine and running the corresponding hacking program by typing its name and a port number (e.g. "FTPHack 21"). Once you're in, your job is to either snoop through some files for a password, to download files, or to delete them using basic terminal skills. You're supposed to cover your tracks by deleting logs, but it rarely matters. The same thing, over and over, no brains required. There's no sense you're accomplishing anything of value, nor of any consequence to yourself or others.

It's an insult to anyone with more than a surface-level understanding of network security, as challenging to a puzzle gamer as 50 consecutive games of Tic-tac-toe, and isn't even that interesting in terms of Hollywood hacking simulations. It's on par with a budding game developer's first project, not something worth spending $10 to $24 on. If you want an intellectual challenge (Hollywood setting, but real problem-solving), check out Zachtronics (Exapunks, Shenzhen I/O, TIS-100).

That said, Hacknet does have a few high points. The music is pretty great. The Labyrinths DLC is slightly less mediocre, but isn't worth the regular $7 price point on top of the base game's $10. If everything was like the DLC's final mission — which unexpectedly drops you into a timed, high-stakes situation with dire consequences — this might actually be a decent game. As is, though, it's just a bland waste of money.

If you want an intellectual challenge (Hollywood setting, but real problem-solving), check out Zachtronics (Exapunks, Shenzhen I/O, TIS-100). That said, Hacknet does have a few high points. The music is pretty great. The Labyrinths DLC is slightly less mediocre, but isn't worth the regular $7 price point on top of the base game's $10. If everything was like the DLC's final mission — which unexpectedly drops you into a timed, high-stakes situation with dire consequences — this might actually be a decent game. As is, though, it's just a bland waste of money.

As that user, it’s up to you to unravel the mystery and ensure that Hacknet-OS doesn't fall into the wrong hands.

Exploring the volatile nature of personal privacy, the prevalence of corporate greed, and the hidden powers of hackers on the internet, Hacknet delivers a true hacking simulation, while offering a support system that allows total beginners get a grasp of the real-world applications and commands found throughout the game.

review_text_raw:
There are clear influences from Uplink, but Hacknet stands on its own two feet for many design decisions.

Hacknet requires a lot of typing due to the text console. This brings a level of realism which is enjoyable, and the countdown timers do not seem to require the player to type at 200 words per minute. However, a few actions can also be initiated by mouse using a graphical user interface. The use of the mouse is a bit incoherent: those features which can use the mouse and those which cannot feel arbitrary and without obvious design merit.

There are a number of little bugs here and there. Head over to the discussions and check the bug report thread. Many of the valid bugs reported actually have more to do with polish. It's unfair to call them bugs, but fixing the issues could enhance the game's polish and lead to better immersion. There are a few actual bugs that can lead to gameplay issues, but they seem to be few and far between.

The story is a bit linear. I have found it hard to explore the networked universe outside where the missions take me. Compare this to Uplink, where there are a great many ways to find and access computers by goofing around. Computers tend to have random snippets from bash.org , which are humorous logs of conversations that reportedly happened on IRC. It's a nice touch as a reward for looking at systems and it makes them feel a little more fleshed out, yet the contents tend to be disconnected from any of the game's context. The snippets simultaneously help and hurt immersion.

Creative expression is available in small doses, but I do not consider this any kind of sandbox game. The potential for such a thing is there. For example, there are computers which run web servers. You can modify the HTML, and when you visit the web server, your changes are visible. It can be amusing to deface a virtual server even if no other living being will see it. However, if you delete all the system files from a computer and then forcibly shut it down, it should prevent the system from rebooting. This would destroy a system. In Hacknet, if you do this, the system will disappear from your network map for a little while and then come back (while still lacking system files). As a related polish-bug: you can immediately connect to any computer "destroyed" this way using the command console, even if the network map does not show the system as online.

The music is electronica-themed to suit the stereotype of a computer hacker. The sound track brings good ambience. I personally start to notice the repetitious nature of the music after playing 2-3 solid hours, but that's usually a good time to take a break anyway.

The recent release for Linux/Mac is welcome, except that has introduced a number of new bugs that need to be squashed. Save game interoperability is a current problem that needs to be resolved at the time of this writing. Linux/Mac support has its own thread in the game's Steam discussion area. I'm sure those problems will be resolved soon enough, but they are worth reading through before purchasing if you plan to play on Mac or Linux.

Overall, I'd say Hacknet is a fun puzzle game with a solid computer hacker theme. It could use more polish and the design decisions regarding keyboard or mouse interfacing could use some rethinking. As a professional programmer and IT person, I cannot really say with certainty if this game is accessible to non-programmers or non-IT people. I suspect the game is approachable enough to anyone who has ever had to type commands into anything instead of clicking glittery UI buttons.

review_text_raw:
I'll say it straight, I am not a hacker or an expert programmer, although I had a minimal use of console clients and some programming basics, beside using consoles like DOS in my very first PCs. Hacknet is a hacking game entirely done through console commands and minimal interface in a fictional OS, you'll join tasks to do to go through a main story and a few side jobs, most of the game is all about typing codes on console, the faster you go the better you hack, there are just a few times you must stop and think how to proceed to get the informations or files you need, which is nothing impossible for a beginner. I liked this game for it's way to be different, not too difficult to learn, not too far from reality. 


[b][u]PROS[/u][/b]
[list]

[*][u]HACKING[/u]: There's not much space for hacking effects, beside a few simple animations, hacking goes all through a console, and that's the way real hackers work! The way it makes you feel is great, with some basic commands you can do anything you want without being an IT expert, actually teaching one thing or two about real hacking and consoles! I enjoyed this version of hacking better than unrealistic interactive ways from other games, thumbs up!

[*][u]DIFFICULTY[/u]: Difficulty is very balanced, at least for someone with my experience, it's all about learning a dozen commands, understand what they do and use them for your purposes, not too hard, neither too easy. Once you understand how to use them, you need to get faster and use logic to find what you need, which could be a hidden file or password, beginners shouldn't have too many problems, intermediates woul enjoy it, experts maybe would find it a bit too easy and boring.

[*][u]MINIMAL[/u]: Its minimal graphics just plays a good role, real hackers don't use animations and such, leaving it minimal gives it some realism and fashion, plus makes the game lighter. Thanks for leaving it as minimal as it would be in real hacking, with just very few add ons.

[*][u]STORY AND BACKSTORY[/u]: At first I had the feeling it was short and easy...and I was right, although the climax near the end was awesome, got me stuck into knowing the ending of it and hack into the very last hard tasks, I had to change my opinion about the story, it was good and interesting! There's a bit of backstory about the making of the game, explained by the developer himself, which makes the game's finale even better.

[*][u]WORKSHOP[/u]: I noticed the workshop is enabled and has extra missions and stories to download and play. I admit I didn't try anything from the workshop yet, but sounds like you can expand your game with some addons, which compensaty the main story's shortness and the game's price.

[*][u]SMOOTH AND LIGHT[/u]: Being mostly on console and so minimal, the game runs great on PC with very low hardware requirement. As far as the gameplay experience and fun are untouched, it's a good strong point to distribute the game to low end and PCs not made for gaming.


[/list]


[b][u]CONS[/u][/b]
[list]

[*][u]EYE BOILING[/u]: I've spent about 23 years in front of screens, starting from old CRTs, despite that I never had problems with my sight, either glasses or hurting eyes for long times. Despite that, Hacknet was the first and only game to give me eye pain, not fully sure if my sight is just failing or had a tiring day, but it never happened before. Watching the console for a few hours was a lot worse than I ever experienced before. So be careful, you may need some eye resting from time to time or just not play it for too long.

[*][u]END MISSION EMAILS[/u]: Just like real tasks, you don't win as soon as you reach your objective, most of times you need to send an email back to the contact and it will say if you completed your mission or not. Some tasks requires to write a password in the reply, that way you know what you need to find and what you need to write, but most of times it's all about sending a blank email back, if you didn't complete it, you'll get an error while trying to send the email. To cut it short, there are times you just need to access to files or servers and then answer the email, sometimes your objective is not so clear, so you will get stuck in the email before you fry your mind thinking about stuff you may have skipped or fry the game by reading a step-by-step guide, which kills the fun from the game. There were a few times that frustrated me, maybe giving more informations about the task or send back an email to give hints about the missing tasks would have been better.

[*][u]STORY LENGTH[/u]: Even if short and simple, I praised the story for its climax, but I can't hide a bit of disappointment for being so short, about 9-12 hours for the story, 3-4 extra hours to complete achievements and the other contracts and about 3-4 hours for the DLC (which I don't own nor tried). would have been perfect to almost double its time to make the game truly worth its price, but at least the workshop should help a bit more.

[/list]

Final word: Not too easy, not too hard, made for newbies curious about hacking and people with a bit of knowledge about it. If you accept the compromise to "play" on the console only, it will give you a true hacking feeling and about 10 hours of fun, and I loved it. Recommended for those people, especially if you can find it for a good price!

review_text_raw:
Good: 
[list]
    [*]the command line UI is accurate, and makes you feel a lot like a real hacker.
    [*]nice music
    [*]lots of little easter eggs
    [*]technically very accurate (uses correct port numbers, IP addresses, and more)
[/list]

Bad: 
[list]
   [*]core gameplay is extremely repetitive and time consuming (which is an awful combination)
[/list]

The core gameplay of Hacknet revolves around you, a hacker, who can run several different programs to hack into a server and complete some task for a client. For example, hacking into the fried chicken chain CFC server and stealing the list of 11 secret herbs and spices.

It's an interesting concept to start with, however the game falls extremely short in that the gameplay never evolves into anything that is challenging or involves meaningful decision making. 

Hacking each server in the entire game is exactly the same. That is no exaggeration. You literally do the exact same 3-7 things for each server you encounter in order to hack into it. And the worst part about this process is that the "hacking" requires no user interaction. You simply wait 1-2 minutes for the hacking programs to finish, and then you complete whatever task you were assigned to do on the server.

At no point do you need to make any in game decisions when hacking. At no point do you have any decision to make that can affect the gameplay. And that's really where it all falls apart for me. What am I really doing in this game? Because the game really lacks in the feeling of accomplishment.

I can completely understand how this gameplay can appeal to people who want to feel like a hacker, because the game definitely hits the mark in that regard. But once you get past that, you realise there is very little "gameplay" to be had. It just feels like a demo.

This game is definitely fun to play, even though it looks fairly basic at first, and probably won't last you more than 8-15 hours (depending on whether you want to do one playthrough or more).

Your role is that of... yourself, hacker extraordinaire—or something, because in the beginning, your character is probably just fiddling around with their computer. Until they receive an e-mail from Bit, late hacker who's posthumously trying to accomplish what they couldn't do when alive. Armed with a couple of commands and utilities, it's time to jump into the game, a game that may turn out to be bigger than you'd think.

Through a series of e-mails and missions, you get introduced gradually to other hackers, become part of hacking groups, and discover what's hiding behind the Bit case. The game is fairly straightforward in that regard (get a mission, hack ports, hack your way in, steal/delete data, delete logs, disconnect), and getting the tools you need isn't hard, however most of the computers you discover along the way also contain other files you can read, such as IRC logs, and part of the fun I had came from exploring. You also have to make a few choices that may affect which missions are available to you—for instance, accepting missions from another hacker will prevent you from taking another hacker's contracts—as well as a couple of other choices about more ethically-challenged assignments.

The interface is simple enough, in a "minimalist OS" way, with a few animations when running hacking utilities; I quite liked that, as seeing more "Holywood hacking animations" wouldn't have been very believable (but not displaying anything would, on the other hand, be a bit boring). I didn't really like the window with nodes representing all the computers you could access, though: it was nice in the beginning, then became seriously cluttered (in the end, I'd just type the IP addresses directly in the terminal, it was faster).

Interestingly, if you've never worked with Unix-based workstations, or Linux, this can actually be a nice little introduction to that kind of OS. Very basic, obviously, with commands that don't even need any arguments; still, since a lot of what you have to do in game is terminal-based, be ready to type fast and work with commands much more than with just clicking on buttons (being used to TABbing my way both in bash and on IOS, I was totally fine with that, and most often I would be faster this way). Getting the hang of this isn't very difficult, and even if you know nothing to running commands, the game will easily make you feel like you do.

Sounds and music: mostly music, with one voiceover at a given point, and alerts when you're getting traced. At first, I feared the audio tracks would become repetitive; in the long run, they fit pretty well, with appropriate change of tracks when you get into a new hacking group or attempt a new kind of operation, and provided good background music without being intrusive.

Problems I noticed: the game runs in full-screen and would crash when I alt-tabbed out of it. Not sure if it's just my computer, or systematic. It didn't detract from my enjoyment, so I admit I didn't pay much attention (and didn't exactly *have to* alt-tab out of it anyway, since the immersion is much better if you don't).

Awaiting the next DLC now? I also wouldn't mind multiplayer possibilities, like hacking each other, or having to form alliances. That would be fun as well.

Conclusion: Recommended.

What a great game. I acquired this in a Humble Bundle recently with a few other titles. Without looking, I assumed it was just a game that was shoveled in to fluff out the bundle, and that I wouldn't enjoy it. I ended up loving it, and I'm definitely going to buy the DLC (and likely any more content that may come out for Hacknet in the future).

Hacknet, for lack of better words, is a Unix-based hacking simulator in which you use the combination of a point-and-click interface and a command prompt to explore the mysterious death of a hacker named "Bit." Bit has arranged to send automated messages to you posthumously, giving you leads that are just enough for you to find your way.

Being not much of a programmer, and unfamiliar with Linux and Unix-based command systems (idk man I just look stuff up and punch shit into the Windows 10 command prompt and sometimes it says words back to me), I felt learning to play Hacknet might be too daunting of a task. However, the feeling subsided in less than half an hour, when I was able to navigate through any device's file systems with ease, hopping from device to device, opening ports, cracking passwords, etc. Not long after that was I very immersed in the story (something I have a hard time being in MANY games).

While some aspects of the game can be done through clicking between devices, folders, and apps, other things are seemingly only possible by using the command-line, keeping the game immersive and making you feel, in a sense, accomplished. YOU cracked open all of Macrosoft's ports and got to snoop around in their sensitive files. YOU found a security loophole by exploiting a computer's connected smartphone. YOU made a clean getaway just in time before having your IP traced, clearing the system logs and running for the hills with some juicy new program you can use to hack *even more* devices. And you did it all with your analytical skills and an intuitive command system. In fact, there's even a point in the game where your OS/interface is essentially deleted from your system by another angry hacker, leaving you with a big black command terminal, having to plot through your own computer to restore the deleted files and get yourself back in the game. Just like in real life, each device you access seems like a sum of its parts, even your own.

The IP tracing mechanic is excellent, and pretty much exactly what you'd imagine seeing on some Hollywood hacker's monitor. It keeps the pressure on, even if it is slow at times. RAM management, learning what ports to use when, and being able to type quickly and remember which programs do what are important, and make hacking into each and every system rewarding in its own way, even if it doesn't have quite what you were looking for.

The visual effects are excellent, if a bit cheesy at times. The interface is simple enough that these "glitchy" or "tech-y" effects aren't too jarring unless they need to be, which keeps the game immersive but also fun to watch. I'd advise that anyone with epilepsy be careful with this game at some times - lots of effects are fast or flashy in nature.

The story doesn't seem to thrust itself into your face at all. Save for the occasional automated (but justified) email from Bit, you discover all of the story on your own, and every lead and new piece of information feels genuine and is worth discovering.

Overall, I had a lot of fun with this game. Two complaints (which end up not really being complaints after I explain them):

- The IP map, showing all known devices and their IPs, can get a bit cluttered, and it's easy to forget where one particular computer is on the big web of spinning circles and lines connecting them. The position of an IP address on the map is not always intuitive. However, this could arguably help with immersion, making you feel like you're navigating through a web of IP addresses. It's the internet in its raw form - not catered to your viewing pleasure.

- I'm left wanting more. Not that I didn't get my money's worth, but I want more. But that's something every game should strive for - leaving you wanting more, and not outstaying its welcome.

Challenging, but *very* rewarding command system that makes you feel clever. Decent story that keeps you invested throughout the game. Findable humorous IRC logs, detailing early Internet culture, which I think are ripped straight from Bash.org, meaning they are real logs written by real people. Stereotypical electronic "hacker" soundtrack which helps the atmosphere of the game.

If any of this interests you, definitely get Hacknet, especially if it's in a bundle or on sale.

Hacknet is the lone developer's pet project, and it saddens me to give it a negative rating. Honestly, though, I just didn't enjoy the game at all. It is extraordinarily repetitive, and after a while, it feels that you're doing nothing except waiting for hacking animations to finish. With only 2 exceptions, [i] every [/i] mission can be beaten by typing the same 6-7 commands in a predetermined order. After 2-3 hours of gameplay, I kept asking myself, "why is every mission the same, and why am I being forced to do it again and again?"

I did enjoy the jokes hidden in the IRC chat logs, but even then, they repeated themselves. If you read every IRC log in the game, you'd run across the same exact joke (literally) 4-5 times. It's a bit disappointing that the developer couldn't even populate the IRC logs with unique jokes. 

As an alternative criticism... the UI has some definite issues. For example, the node map gets so cluttered that it becomes completely unusable. You're constantly forced to backtrack and look at the mission statement in order to remind yourself which nodes should be broken into. It's very frustrating, and definitely killed my sense of immersion.

All in all, I can't recommend this game. I understand that others love it, but honestly, it just wasn't for me.

review_text_raw:
This game is pretty dope.

Gameplay-wise, the actual inputs you'll perform are mainly terminal based. Most of the time you'll be typing commands as rapidly as you can. Actual inputs can be tricky if you need to operate quickly, but the majority of what you'll be doing is essentially puzzle solving. A typical mission in the game requires you to gain access to a given entry point which will contain links or clues that you can follow to the next point, which may contain further clues, etc. That's an incredibly basic description of the game: Actual missions are immersive enough and the actual hints/puzzles/solutions are varied enough that the game is able to stay fresh well through the main campaign and DLC.

The story is pretty cool. (Won't go into spoilers here, what I tell you is what you learn literally within minutes of starting the game.) A notorious hacker who goes by Bit has passed away, and has left you his custom-made hacking software in his wake, along with the request to use it to figure out what killed him and why. You quickly integrate with a local hacker group and start climbing the ranks to gain influence and leads. Along the way you'll acquire (either from your hacker group or by stealing it from a target computer) new tools or methods that allow you to break into more secure devices. Since the game is all text based, you'll only get to know characters via what they've written to you, and it can be tricky to build strong characters that way if the player is impatient. I feel that sticking through and reading the text will greatly benefit your enjoyment of the story of the game as well as of the game overall.

The aesthetic of the game is a big part of it. The entire game is played as though it's not a game. It's as if you have a virtual machine running another OS on your computer. The perspective is never pulled into real life, and you'll never see your character because as far as the game is concerned, YOU in real life are your character. This is an excellent way to build immersion, and you'll find yourself quickly sucked in to the game. The visuals are simplistic but robust and well designed (and even customizable, eventually), and the soundtrack will keep you cool while trying to break into complex systems and get you pumped when it's time to move fast. Just playing the game and becoming immersed is a bit of an experience that can be hard to find elsewhere.

As an aside, I would reccomend the DLC if you enjoy the main game. It tells a story that's basically completely separate from the main game: Essentially it may as well be a sequel. It introduces new systems that compliment the puzzle elements like I mentioned above. The game also features workshop support which contains even more community made campaigns (some as long as the DLC), but many of them require content from the DLC to function.

Tl;dr: Fun game, you'll get immersed if you let yourself and it's a serious blast. Gameplay is essentially puzzle based but at times requires you to be fast too.

review_text_raw:
[i]Note: I am biased because of the nature of my job. While not related to IT Security, it involves technical troubleshooting / problem solving and all kind of investigations. Basically, less fun version of Hacknet.[/i]

[h3]Accurate Hacking Simulator?[/h3]

I was not exposed to a lot of hacking in games, maybe just a bit in Sleeping Dogs, or Cyberpunk 2077. While other games focus purely on hacking vibes, those tend to ignore the actual process. And Hacknet pays much more attention to the realistic aspect of the game.

Of course, to me it looks like huge oversimplification, but that was made as a game, right? It was made to be simple, fun and accessible. And it never felt like I am working, it felt like I am playing a game and having a good time. So while not being accurate, it nails the realistic hacking experience to enough extent. 

[h3]Handholding or Exploration?[/h3]

The first 60% to 70% percent of the game felt like a tutorial. Fun, with a lot of stories and action, but with a huge sense that I am playing in a sandbox. Everything is pretty safe, and you get what you need to do right from the email, so you need to execute specific steps without much investigation. Yes, you need to look for something specific, but it is usually very algorithmic and follows the same steps. 

So, this feels like handholding to me, and having to "detective" part to it, where you just don't know where to look at and have to think and explore. 

But! There are endgame quests, such as the main story line or Project Junebug quest. Those actually did things perfectly as I have wanted. There is more to reading, investigating, searching and connecting pieces of information together. This was perfect. 

Example: usually it would be "find a (file / password / IP) or edit / remove something. Here is the server.". That is straightforward. 

Project Junebug: Here is the name of the person. Kill him. 

You see what I mean? That is perfect example of what I wanted this game to be. And it eventually has things that appeal to me! So, overall, great experience. Right?

[h3]A bit of so-so moments[/h3]

Just one. The game has netMap, a graph that displays the machines you have connected to. And the graph grows, and there is less and less space, it all  becomes cluttered at some point. And there is no way to clean it up, resize, organize or alter. And this is sad a bit, because the missions that I liked involve a lot of research, but the research progress was hevily impacted by overall messy navigation system. 

But it's a minor thing. What else?


[h3]The Easter Eggs and Secrets[/h3]

While the big part of the game feels like a tutorial, it has a lot of things to explore. Jokes and memes, hidden quests with high rewards - it's all there. So if you want, you can take much more from the game than it offers at a first sight.

Like in some RPGs you can even get overpowered pretty early - if you follow some clues in the game, you can get CLOCK.EXE, which makes game itself hacked. Things that are hidden and require exploration definitely cool here.

[h3]The Music[/h3]

I pay a lot of attention to game OSTs, it makes me love the game more if the music resonates with me. And back in 2017 when I have bought the game, I learned about Hacknet from Remi (The Algorithm) - one of the musicians behind the OST, and I bought it. So, to me the OST is perfectly fitting the game. Just very neat, I thought. Until the final mission.

I have three examples of getting goosebumps from the music in the game:
1. One optional boss fight in Baldur's Gate 3
2. Expedition 33 in various places.

And... Yeah, the final mission of Hacknet! Putting [spoiler]Carpenter Brut's Roller Mobster[/spoiler], one of my favorite synthwave / darksynth tracks ever made me freeze for a minute in awe. And then realize that time is ticking and I need to do everything fast. Perfect sense of adrenaline. Great choice for OST!

[h3]Really solid hacking-lite experience[/h3]

Overall, I liked this game. Relatively short, but never gets dull. And I have not even touched the DLC yet - and it has 97% positive rating! So, while the main game is over for me, I will get to Labyrinths in future to feel this enjoyment again.

So, this feels like handholding to me, and having to "detective" part to it, where you just don't know where to look at and have to think and explore. But! There are endgame quests, such as the main story line or Project Junebug quest. Those actually did things perfectly as I have wanted. There is more to reading, investigating, searching and connecting pieces of information together. This was perfect. Example: usually it would be "find a (file / password / IP) or edit / remove something. Here is the server.". That is straightforward. Project Junebug: Here is the name of the person. Kill him. You see what I mean? That is perfect example of what I wanted this game to be. And it eventually has things that appeal to me! So, overall, great experience. Right? [h3]A bit of so-so moments[/h3] Just one. The game has netMap, a graph that displays the machines you have connected to. And the graph grows, and there is less and less space, it all becomes cluttered at some point. And there is no way to clean it up, resize, organize or alter. And this is sad a bit, because the missions that I liked involve a lot of research, but the research progress was hevily impacted by overall messy navigation system. But it's a minor thing. What else? [h3]The Easter Eggs and Secrets[/h3] While the big part of the game feels like a tutorial, it has a lot of things to explore. Jokes and memes, hidden quests with high rewards - it's all there. So if you want, you can take much more from the game than it offers at a first sight. Like in some RPGs you can even get overpowered pretty early - if you follow some clues in the game, you can get CLOCK.EXE, which makes game itself hacked. Things that are hidden and require exploration definitely cool here. [h3]The Music[/h3] I pay a lot of attention to game OSTs, it makes me love the game more if the music resonates with me. And back in 2017 when I have bought the game, I learned about Hacknet from Remi (The Algorithm) - one of the musicians behind the OST, and I bought it. So, to me the OST is perfectly fitting the game. Just very neat, I thought. Until the final mission. I have three examples of getting goosebumps from the music in the game: 1. One optional boss fight in Baldur's Gate 3 2. Expedition 33 in various places. And... Yeah, the final mission of Hacknet! Putting [spoiler]Carpenter Brut's Roller Mobster[/spoiler], one of my favorite synthwave / darksynth tracks ever made me freeze for a minute in awe. And then realize that time is ticking and I need to do everything fast. Perfect sense of adrenaline. Great choice for OST! [h3]Really solid hacking-lite experience[/h3] Overall, I liked this game. Relatively short, but never gets dull. And I have not even touched the DLC yet - and it has 97% positive rating! So, while the main game is over for me, I will get to Labyrinths in future to feel this enjoyment again.

At first, I really loved it. Felt like a new version of Uplink. Hacking itself seemed interesting and there was a simple story behind it. What's not to like?

Unfortunately, it started to be too repetitive after a while. Hacking doesn't require any skill, you just use the same apps over and over again. Initially I thought it would change later in the game, but it didn't. I loved the moment when another hacker deleted something from my computer and I had to get it back using only the command line, but this was just a brief part of the game. The rest started to feel really dull. I lost interest in the story, which wasn't really going anywhere by the way, and just stopped playing.

If you can get it cheap, it may be worth a try, but in my opinion it's just a huge waste of potential.

Holy crap. This game immersed me in a way no other game has for a long time. I won't go into the detail of the autheniticity of the simulator or the visuals or sound, as myriads before me have covered that. This game surprised me. Spoiler alert for those who wish to keep reading.

But no, the game rattled to life again and forced me to think about how to restore my own pc, and that is something to be applauded in a game.

I was stressed and terriefied, and it was so, intense! Seriously, go try it for yourself. :)
